defects: Single locked-off equirectangular shot for 20s: no camera move, no cut, no reframing. All motion is simulation advection at a constant rate.
Rainbow/jet colormap for CO2 makes false bands (cyan–yellow–red steps) that read as fronts. The perceptual ordering is non-monotonic and fights the CO gray layer.
Date counter ticks in hard steps with no easing. It is the only typographic motion, and it is purely informational.

Lower-third bar is a dense data-sheet strip: tiny unreadable legend labels and two full colormaps. The NASA logo and office credit compete for attention, and the scale text is soft and illegible at delivery size.
At 100%, compression is soft and smeary, with mushy detail in the high-frequency red filaments and slight blocking in the dark-red regions. Saturated reds clip toward a flat maroon.
The gray carbon-monoxide overlay on the continents is muddy and low-contrast. It reads as a dirty wash, not a distinct layer.
The film starts and ends mid-stream on an arbitrary date, with no opening hold, build or resolve.
gaps: There's no directed choreography or arc. A top studio would art-direct the data: push in on Asian and North American emission plumes, follow a single plume across the Pacific, and build to a hemispheric-scale reveal at around 70%. Here the 20s is one uniform, flat rate of change.

Color and finish: they need a perceptually uniform, restrained palette with a single accent for sources, plus lit 3D globe treatment with atmospheric falloff and clean high-bitrate rendering. This piece has a jet colormap with clipped reds and compression smear.

Type and information design: the legend bar should be replaced with sparse, meaningful annotation that is timed to events (a sources label, a seasonal drawdown callout, a counter whose cadence or weight responds to ppm). The current footer is a static scientific template.
